interviewQuestions.question: Your recursive solution is correct but too slow. How do you decide whether memoization will fix it, and what does it actually cost?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd check first whether the slowness comes from **recomputing the same subproblem repeatedly** — that's the specific signature memoization fixes, and it's not universal. Naive recursive Fibonacci is the textbook case: the recursion tree revisits the same smaller values exponentially many times, so caching each distinct result turns O(2ⁿ) time into O(n).

The cost is an O(n)-ish cache — one entry per distinct subproblem actually reached — on top of whatever stack space the recursion already used. I'd size that before committing to it: if the number of distinct subproblems is small relative to the time saved (as with Fibonacci, where n = 40 fixes an otherwise 10¹²-call blowup with just 40 cache entries), it's an easy yes. If the state space is enormous — say the subproblem is keyed by a large multi-dimensional index — the cache itself could become the new bottleneck, and I'd want to check that against available memory before assuming caching is free.

Concretely I'd say: 'this recomputes fib(k) roughly 2^(n-k) times for each k — I'll add a cache keyed by n, dropping time to O(n) for an O(n) memory cost,' rather than just 'I'll memoize it' without the reasoning.

**Testing:** whether you diagnose the actual pattern (redundant recomputation) rather than reaching for memoization as a reflex whenever recursion is slow.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: When would you choose to precompute a full lookup table versus computing each answer on demand and caching it as you go?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It comes down to how much of the possible input space I actually expect to be queried, and whether I know that ahead of time.

If I know the query universe is small and fixed — say, 'is n prime?' for every n from 1 to a known bound N, and I'll be asked this many times — precomputing a sieve once, up front, at O(N log log N), turns every later query into an O(1) lookup. The upfront cost is justified because I know it will be amortized across many queries.

If instead the universe of possible inputs is huge but only a small, unpredictable subset will ever actually be queried — say, checking primality for arbitrary large numbers that arrive one at a time — precomputing everything wastes enormous memory on answers nobody asked for. Memoizing on demand (compute an answer the first time it's needed, cache it, reuse it if asked again) gets the same eventual per-query speed for whatever's actually been queried, without paying for the rest of the space.

The deciding question I'd actually ask out loud: 'do we know the full query universe ahead of time, and will we exhaust most of it?' If yes, precompute. If the query pattern is sparse or unknown, memoize lazily instead.

**Testing:** whether you can reason about query volume and universe size as the actual decision variable, rather than treating 'precompute everything' as always the more thorough answer.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Trade-offs

interviewQuestions.question: A teammate wants to add a hash map to speed up a lookup inside a hot loop. What would make you push back, if anything?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
My default reaction is actually to support it — a linear scan inside a loop turning O(n²) into O(n) via a hash map is one of the highest-leverage, lowest-risk changes available, and I'd want to know the concrete before/after ("O(n) extra memory, O(n²) drops to O(n) time") to confirm it's worth it, which for any non-trivial n it almost always is.

Where I would push back: if the collection being checked is genuinely tiny and bounded — say, always under 10 elements — the constant-factor overhead of hashing (computing a hash, probing a bucket) can plausibly lose to a short linear scan, and introducing a hash map there adds a hashability requirement and a little memory for no measurable win. I'd also push back if the values being hashed are mutable objects being used as keys — that's a correctness bug waiting to happen (lookups silently break after the key mutates), not just a performance question, and I'd flag it before the trade-off discussion even starts.

Outside of those two cases — genuinely tiny collections, or a mutability/hashability problem — I'd support the change and just ask that we state the trade-off explicitly in the PR description rather than leave it implicit.

**Testing:** whether you evaluate a proposed optimization on its actual merits and edge cases, rather than reflexively approving or reflexively distrusting a hash-map suggestion.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Code review

interviewQuestions.question: You've memoized a recursive function and it's fast enough, but now memory is the constraint. What's your next move?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd check whether the trade can run in reverse: instead of caching every subproblem's result, keep only whichever small, fixed set of prior results the next step actually needs, and discard the rest.

Fibonacci is again the clean example: a full memoization table keeps all n prior results, but `fib(n)` only ever depends on `fib(n-1)` and `fib(n-2)` — so two rolling variables, updated each step, give the identical O(n) time with O(1) space instead of O(n). This is the mirror image of memoization: recomputing (or rather, never discarding what's about to be needed) versus deliberately throwing away everything except the minimum required state.

More generally, I'd look at the dependency structure of the memoized recurrence: if each subproblem only ever depends on a small, bounded window of prior subproblems (not the entire history), the full cache is more than the algorithm actually needs, and a rolling window replaces it. If instead the dependency structure is genuinely irregular — later subproblems depend on arbitrary earlier ones — the full cache usually can't be shrunk without changing the algorithm's actual guarantees, and I'd say so rather than force a fix that doesn't fit.

The same lever shows up at a much larger scale in gradient checkpointing for deep learning, which recomputes intermediate activations during backprop instead of storing all of them, trading extra compute for a large cut in GPU memory — same idea, different domain.

**Testing:** whether you can run the space-time trade-off in the direction the situation actually needs, rather than only knowing the 'spend memory to save time' half of it.
